SpatialRehab

Errorless-learning cognitive rehab for early-stage dementia, built for Apple Vision Pro.

  • visionOS 2.0+
  • SwiftUI
  • RealityKit
  • Swift Charts

Design overview · August 2026

The problem

Dementia takes the everyday first.

For someone in moderate cognitive decline, the hardest part of the day is the ordinary part. Long before anything dramatic, the small skills that hold a day together begin to fray.

Routines

Morning steps fall out of order. Medication is missed, or taken twice.

Wayfinding

A walk taken for thirty years suddenly stops feeling familiar.

Identity

Faces stay warm, but the names attached to them start to slip.

Our clinical foundation

Errorless learning.
The patient is never set up to fail.

Every screen in SpatialRehab is checked against one principle from dementia-rehabilitation research: support arrives before a mistake can happen, and it steps back as confidence returns.

Cue first

Prompts appear before a wrong answer is possible, never as a correction after one.

Reinforce, never punish

No red marks, no failure states, no score ever shown to the patient. Even a tally can read as pass or fail.

Fade gradually

Cues reduce over spaced repetitions, so ability transfers to real life instead of the headset.

The product

One calm window. One clear next step.

  • A single window, never a wall of choices. One activity is offered at a time.
  • Short sessions of 20 to 30 minutes, in line with Apple’s headset guidance.
  • The window steps aside during immersive exercises, so the room itself becomes the interface.

Good afternoon.

First run

Eight small games. One honest baseline.

Before anything else, a short battery gently measures where the patient is today, so every later session has something real to compare against. Played in this order, warm-up first.

01

Reaction Time

Tap the shape the moment it appears.

02

Orientation

Day, month and time of day, asked live and never from a script.

03

Word Memory

Study a short list, then recognise it in a grid. No typing.

04

Digit Span

Watch four digits flash, tap them back in order.

05

Pattern Matching

Classic memory pairs. Mismatches simply turn back over.

06

Trail Making

Connect scattered numbers in order, at your own pace.

07

Arithmetic

Single-digit sums, tap the answer, one at a time.

08

Clock Drawing

Draw a clock face freehand. Kept for caregiver review, never auto-scored.

Results are stored for caregivers and the recommendation engine. The patient sees encouragement, never a number.

The flagship exercise

Remember the Way.

A real OpenStreetMap extract of Tiong Bahru, procedurally meshed at runtime, with shophouses, road ribbons, street lamps and trees, then mounted as a miniature on a holographic tabletop.

STUDY

The route draws itself

The path animates along the tabletop and repeats, so it has a chance to encode.

RECALL

Trace it from memory

The map locks and the person draws the route back. Scored by distance from the real polyline, never shown as pass or fail.

STEP INSIDE

Walk it at life size

The miniature scales up around them. Seated pinch-and-hold to move, constant velocity, blink-cut turns, spoken guidance throughout.

Identity

“Who am I?”
Always one tap away.

A personal name card the patient can open at any moment: their photo, their name, the people who love them. It flips to a family tree, and a pinch on a face plays a short greeting from home.

A wider “My People” reminiscence module, with photo cards of familiar faces and a short note on each, already exists in the codebase and is next in line to be wired into navigation.

For caregivers

Progress you can actually see.

  • Every session is kept, not overwritten, giving a real history to compare against the baseline.
  • One trend line per game, plus a gallery of every clock drawing over time.
  • Raw data sits one tap deeper. The dashboard reads plainly, and the detail is there when a clinician wants it.

Adaptive by design

It notices what’s hardest,
and meets the patient there.

Each game maps to a cognitive domain. The recommendation engine ranks domains by measured weakness and suggests what to practise next. It is a plain, explainable calculation, because a caregiver deserves to see exactly why.

Memory
0.61
Executive function
0.38
Numeracy
0.22
priority = 1 − score

Not a black box: no trained model, no hidden weights. The weakest domain surfaces first, and the reasoning is visible at a glance. Values shown are illustrative.

Evidence-based

Calibrated to the research,
not to the demo.

Session length, cadence and program duration come from published dementia-intervention findings and Apple’s own headset-comfort guidance, not from what looks good on stage.

20–30 min

Per session, within Apple’s guidance for continuous headset use.

3× / week

Or more. The intervention cadence with the strongest measured outcomes.

5–8 weeks

Program length where the evidence is strongest. Longer isn’t necessarily better.

A hackathon prototype, not a medical device. Not clinically validated, and making no diagnostic claims. The battery borrows structure from established concepts (clock drawing, digit span, orientation); its specific content is still pending clinical review.
